lines.text: Monday morning. Four agents in four terminals, on four projects, and you are the one holding it all together.
You copy the plan from one chat to the next, answer each prompt in its own window, and check every terminal to find who's stuck. Step away, and everything waits.
Agent R Q is one place for all of them. A workspace per project, one board for every agent, memory they keep, work that starts itself, and your yes, wherever you are.
When one chat holds every project, the agent has to guess which repo a task is about.
So each project gets a workspace. Ada names this one billing, points it at the repo's folder, and starts its mission from a template.
The setup guide gives each agent its exact config: Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, or any A C P agent. One M C P config, with this workspace's own token.
Codex connects, and billing turns green. Each workspace card names the agent working in it.
Hand billing a task, and only billing's agent gets it. Its token works for this workspace, and no other.
Writing a task down is often slower than the work: a title, a paragraph, the same steps as yesterday.
Press N anywhere for a new task, and skip the title. A small model, right in the browser, names it from the description.
Or click the mic, and just say it. On a computer, Whisper turns your voice into text in the browser.
Type a hash and a preset's name, and the message you send every day drops in.
And by default, a reply waits five seconds before it goes, so Cancel can still catch the typo.
A big feature needs five agents, and you end up as the glue, relaying the plan and every question between them.
The Panno is a board of markdown docs that every workspace shares. Ada posts the kickoff note, one checkbox per action item.
Then she asks the supervisor, in the chat box below the board, to split the work and run in parallel whatever can.
It creates a task in each workspace, and four agents start at once. Each item on the note now shows its owner, and the live status of its task.
When the web agent needs the A P I contract, it reads the doc the A P I agent posted, and asks its question right on it.
As the tasks finish, the boxes tick themselves, and the supervisor reports back. Nobody asked you to relay a thing.
One agent finished an hour ago. One has waited forty minutes for your yes. A terminal tells you nothing until you go and look.
Here, every workspace is a card: the agent in it, a green dot while it's connected, and the actions waiting on you, in yellow.
The Kanban board puts every workspace's tasks on one board, and it moves live. No refresh.
When an agent wants to run a command, the request comes to you, with the exact command. Allow and Deny sit right on its card.
Every task keeps a timeline, so you see how long it worked, how long it was blocked, and how long it waited on you.
And the trajectory keeps every tool call on the record: what ran, and who said yes.
Your agent spends an hour learning that the billing tests need Postgres on port five four three three. Tomorrow, a new session learns it again.
Here, before it marks a task done, the agent saves what the next task should know, as one short note in the workspace memory.
The next task starts by loading that memory, and goes straight to the right port.
Playbooks become skills: one copy in your account, switched on per workspace. When an agent adds a missing step, every workspace gets it at once.
Share a workspace's memory with your team, and the lessons one agent learns, every teammate's agent can read.
Every morning you type the same prompts. And every change, you carry from one agent to the next by hand.
Put a task on a schedule: daily at nine, read last night's errors. Each run is a normal task, with its own thread.
Events hand work on. When billing's agent publishes A P I changed, docs and mobile get their tasks at once.
Webhooks let GitHub start the work: a failed build on main becomes a task, before anyone wakes up.
And a workflow chains it all, so a whole release runs step by step, across workspaces.
Close the laptop lid, and your agents stop. Step away, and a prompt waits in a terminal all afternoon.
Enroll the machines you own, with two commands. Each one shows up green, with its C P U and memory.
Start an agent from the browser, in the workspace's folder on that machine. Its terminal opens live, right in the page.
When an agent needs you, a toast finds you on any page. Push, email and Slack reach you with the tab closed.
For the work you trust, Always Allow saves a rule, and Yolo runs a task without asking. The trajectory still records every call.
A workspace per project, handoffs in seconds, and agents that work together. Every agent on one screen, memory they keep, work that starts itself, and any machine you own.
Each of these has its own video in this series. Which would you hand to your agents first? Tell us in the comments. Agent R Q is open source: try it at Agent R Q dot com.
